## `engineBuildId`

```cpp
const char * engineBuildId()
```

 The running engine's build id.

 Derived from the public headers' contents plus the target triple, the build
 type and every flag that changes the engine's symbol surface or type layout
 (currently profiling). Regenerated by the build whenever any of those move,
 so it cannot claim compatibility it does not have.

## `kModuleBuildIdSymbol`

```cpp
inline constexpr const char * kModuleBuildIdSymbol = "hp_module_build_id"
```

 The symbol every gameplay module exports carrying the id it was built with.

 Named here rather than in the loader so that the engine and whatever loads
 modules cannot disagree about it. The loader resolves this, then hands the
 value to `checkModuleBuildId` — which is what keeps the check independent of
 *how* a module was loaded (`dlopen`, `LoadLibrary`, a test harness, or
 whatever T0048 ends up building).

## `ModuleCompatibility`

```cpp
struct ModuleCompatibility
```

 Outcome of a compatibility check.

 `message` is populated on failure and is meant to be shown to a developer
 verbatim: it names the module, both ids, and what to rebuild. A refusal that
 does not say what to do is only marginally better than the corruption it
 prevents.

## `checkModuleBuildId`

```cpp
ModuleCompatibility checkModuleBuildId(const char * module_id)
```

 Compare a module's stamped id against the running engine's.

 Deliberately **equal-or-refuse**. There is no version negotiation, no
 compatibility window and no "minor versions are compatible" — D12's lockstep
 means there is exactly one right answer at any moment, and every mechanism
 for expressing a range is a mechanism that has to be maintained and reasoned
 about. If lockstep is ever abandoned, this design is the wrong starting point
 anyway.

 @param module_id the value of the module's `hp_module_build_id` symbol. May
        be null, which is what a module built without the stamp looks like —
        that is a refusal, not a pass, because an unstamped module is the case
        with no evidence either way rather than the case that is probably fine.
 @returns whether the module may be loaded, plus both ids for reporting.

## `describeIncompatibility`

```cpp
const char * describeIncompatibility(const char * module_name, ModuleCompatibility result)
```

 Build the developer-facing refusal text for a failed check.

 Separate from the check so a caller can decide where it goes — the editor
 wants it in a panel, the runtime in a log, a test in an assertion message.
 @param module_name shown to the developer so the message names which module
        was refused; may be null, rendered as `<module>`.
 @param result the outcome from `checkModuleBuildId`.
 @returns a pointer to a thread-local buffer, valid until the next call on the
          same thread. Not owned by the caller and not freed.
